items.explanation: Grady's 'New South' creed called for diversified industry to replace the old reliance on slavery and cotton agriculture. He declared the South of slavery 'dead.' He preached reunion with the North, not a second secession. He actively courted Northern capital and investment.
items.fact_source: PD: Grady, 'The New South' speech, Dec 1886 — 'The old South rested everything on slavery and agriculture... The new South presents... a diversified industry' + PD portrait (stimulus)

option_explanations.A: Grady declared the South of slavery dead; he did not call for its restoration.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Diversified industry replacing dependence on cotton agriculture was the core of the New South creed.
option_explanations.C: Grady preached reunion with the North, not secession.
option_explanations.D: Grady actively courted Northern investment in Southern enterprises.

options: (A) restore slavery as the basis of the Southern economy
(B) abandon its dependence on cotton agriculture and build diversified industry like the North's
(C) secede from the Union a second time
(D) refuse all Northern investment in Southern enterprises

items.explanation: Grady carried his message to Northerners deliberately: by proclaiming the old South dead, he reassured Northern capital that the South was stable, loyal, and open for investment. He accepted the war's outcome rather than opposing it. His whole argument was that the South needed industry because agriculture alone had failed. The speech says nothing about racial attitudes, and declaring slavery dead is not the same as declaring prejudice dead.
items.fact_source: PD: Grady speech, Dec 1886 (stimulus; delivered to the New England Society, New York City) + PD portrait, ca. 1890 (stimulus)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Addressing Northerners in New York, Grady pitched a changed South worthy of investment and trust.
option_explanations.B: Grady accepted the Civil War's outcome; the speech defends Southern honor, not the Confederate cause.
option_explanations.C: His argument was the reverse: agriculture alone had failed, so the South needed industry.
option_explanations.D: The speech makes no claims about racial attitudes.

options: (A) persuade Northern listeners that the South had changed and was worthy of their investment and trust
(B) announce that he personally opposed the outcome of the Civil War
(C) argue that Southern agriculture had become more profitable than Northern industry
(D) declare that white Southerners had abandoned all racial prejudice

items.explanation: Plantations were indeed divided, but the result was tenancy and sharecropping, not a countryside of independent yeomen: croppers owned no land and worked under the owner's direction. Land ownership remained out of reach for most Southern farmers, Black and white. Agriculture did not end; cotton remained central. Grady was describing the South.
items.fact_source: PD: Grady speech, Dec 1886 (stimulus) + PD: Grimes sharecropping contract, 1882 (croppers owned no land; worked under direction) — tenancy prevalence is general knowledge; flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: Most Southern farmers did not own their land; tenancy and sharecropping dominated.
option_explanations.B: Southern agriculture continued; cotton remained the central crop.
option_explanations.C: The entire speech is about the South's future.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Land was subdivided, but the workers became dependent croppers and tenants rather than independent owners.

options: (A) It was fully accurate: nearly every Southern farmer owned his land by 1890.
(B) It was meaningless because Southern agriculture ended entirely.
(C) It referred to Northern farms, not Southern ones.
(D) It described a real change — plantations were broken into smaller units — but most of those working the land became sharecroppers or tenants, not independent owners.
items.stem: Grady promised 'a hundred farms for every plantation, fifty homes for every palace; and a diversified industry that meets the complex needs of this complex age.' Which statement best evaluates his promise of 'a hundred farms for every plantation'?

stimulus.text: 'The old South rested everything on slavery and agriculture, unconscious that these could neither give nor maintain healthy growth. The new South presents a perfect democracy... a hundred farms for every plantation, fifty homes for every palace; and a diversified industry that meets the complex needs of this complex age.' (Henry W. Grady, 'The New South' speech, December 1886)

items.explanation: The expositions were showcases: Southern boosters displayed factories, machinery, and resources to convince Northern capital that the New South was a safe, profitable place to invest. The Confederacy lost the war; the exposition promoted the new industrial South, not the old cause. It had nothing to do with organizing croppers or tariff protest.
items.fact_source: PD illustration (1895 exposition) + general knowledge: expositions promoted New South industry — flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: The Confederacy lost the war; the exposition promoted the new industrial South.
option_explanations.B: The exposition was a business showcase, not a labor-organizing effort.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Expositions advertised Southern industrial progress to investors and the nation.
option_explanations.D: Tariff protest was not the exposition's purpose.

options: (A) celebrate the Confederacy's victory in the Civil War
(B) organize sharecroppers into labor unions
(C) advertise the New South's industrial progress to Northern investors and the nation
(D) protest federal tariff policies

items.explanation: The enormous purpose-built fairgrounds — manufacturing and electricity buildings included — show how much Atlanta's boosters spent to sell the New South image. It was a local business project, not a federal punishment. The scale demonstrates enthusiasm for industry, not indifference, and the fair courted Northern business rather than protesting it.

option_explanations.C: The exposition's scale demonstrates strong Southern interest in industry.
option_explanations.D: The fair courted Northern business; it did not protest against it.

(C) Few Southerners were interested in industry.

items.explanation: Every clause restricts the cropper: he works under direction, cannot leave for other work, and cannot sell anything until the landowner is paid in full. That is control, not equal bargaining. The contract enforces debt payment rather than abolishing debt. A crop-share tied to one plantation differs from factory wage labor.
items.fact_source: PD: Grimes sharecropping contract, 1882 (key facts from stimulus itself)

option_explanations.A: The contract's restrictions show croppers were not free, equal bargainers.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The contract keeps the cropper's labor and crop under the landowner's control.
option_explanations.C: The contract enforces payment of debts; it does not abolish them.
option_explanations.D: A crop share on a tied plantation is a different arrangement from factory wage labor.

options: (A) Sharecroppers were completely free agents who bargained as equals.
(B) Landowners kept tight control over croppers' labor and crops, leaving them little economic independence.
(C) The contract abolished all debt in farming.
(D) Sharecropping was identical to wage labor in factories.
items.stem: The terms of this contract most strongly support which conclusion about sharecropping?

stimulus.text: 'All must work under my direction.... No sharecropper is to work off the plantation when there is any work for them to do for me. Nothing can be sold from their crops until my rent is all paid, and all amounts they owe me are paid in full.' (Sharecropping contract, Grimes family papers, North Carolina, 1882)

items.explanation: The clause strips the cropper of the central right of a free producer — deciding when and where to sell — and guarantees the landowner is paid before the worker sees anything, reproducing the dependency of slavery in contractual form. No wage is paid; the cropper gets a crop share. He owns no land. The landowner remains central, controlling the sale.
items.fact_source: PD: Grimes contract, 1882 (stimulus) + continuity-with-slavery interpretation (standard historical argument — flagged for audit)

option_explanations.A: No cash wage is paid; the cropper receives a share of the crop.
option_explanations.B: The cropper owns no land under this contract.
option_explanations.C: The landowner controls the sale — his role is central, not ended.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Denying the cropper control of the sale and deducting debts first preserved economic dependency.

options: (A) it paid the cropper a fair cash wage
(B) it gave the cropper full ownership of the land
(C) it ended the landowner's role in farming entirely
(D) it denied the cropper control over selling his own crop and let the landowner deduct debts first — keeping the worker economically dependent, as under slavery

items.explanation: Washington's Atlanta message urged Black Southerners to prove their economic value through work and education while postponing demands for political and social equality — accommodation as a strategy. He counseled patience and labor, not rebellion or land redistribution. He saw economic independence as the way out of dependency, not sharecropping as an ideal.
items.fact_source: PD photograph, ca. 1895 (stimulus) + general knowledge: Washington's 1895 Atlanta address — not in u6.md; flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: Washington counseled work and patience, not rebellion.
option_explanations.B: He did not demand federal land redistribution.
option_explanations.C: Correct. His strategy accepted segregation for the moment while building Black economic strength.
option_explanations.D: He presented economic self-improvement as the escape from dependency, not sharecropping as ideal.

options: (A) a call for immediate violent rebellion
(B) a demand for the federal government to redistribute land
(C) an accommodationist strategy: accepting segregation for now while building Black economic strength
(D) an endorsement of sharecropping as the ideal life

items.explanation: Poll taxes and literacy tests were written in race-neutral language but designed and administered to eliminate Black voting — the legal architecture of Jim Crow. They restricted rather than expanded the franchise. The tax's stated school purpose did not change its function as a voting barrier. Registration of Black voters collapsed under these constitutions.
items.fact_source: PD: Mississippi Constitution, 1890 (stimulus) + u6.md §The story — 'Southern states rewrote constitutions to strip Black citizens of the vote — the legal architecture of Jim Crow'

option_explanations.A: Correct. Race-neutral wording masked provisions designed to strip Black citizens of the vote.
option_explanations.B: These provisions restricted the franchise; they did not expand it.
option_explanations.C: The poll tax functioned as a voting barrier regardless of its stated school purpose.
option_explanations.D: Black voter registration collapsed under these constitutions; it was not encouraged.

options: (A) strip Black citizens of the vote while appearing to apply the rules to everyone
(B) expand voting rights to all Southerners equally
(C) raise money for public schools without affecting elections
(D) encourage Black voter registration

(Sec. 244) These provisions were part of a wave of Southern constitutions rewritten in the 1890s. Their practical purpose was to...

stimulus.text: 'A uniform poll tax of two dollars, to be used in aid of the common schools, and for no other purpose, is hereby imposed on every male inhabitant of this State between the ages of twenty-one and sixty years...' (Constitution of Mississippi, adopted November 1, 1890, Art. 12, Sec. 243). 'On and after the first day of January, A. D., 1892, every elector shall, in addition to the foregoing qualifications, be able to read any section of the constitution of this State; or he shall be able to understand the same when read to him, or give a reasonable interpretation thereof.' (Sec. 244)

items.explanation: Plessy told Southern states that their segregation laws passed constitutional muster — federal blessing for Jim Crow. It entrenched segregation rather than ending it. The case concerned Louisiana, and its doctrine licensed segregation across the South. It withdrew federal protection rather than restoring it.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) — Upheld 'separate but equal'; legal foundation of Jim Crow segregation + §What the exam tests — Contextualization: federal abandonment made Southern white supremacy legally safe again

option_explanations.A: Plessy entrenched segregation; it did not end it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Plessy gave federal approval to Southern segregation laws.
option_explanations.C: The case concerned Louisiana; its principle applied across the South.
option_explanations.D: Plessy withdrew federal protection; it did not restore it.

options: (A) ended segregation in the South immediately
(B) gave federal approval to the segregation laws Southern states were building, making white supremacy legally safe
(C) applied only to Northern states
(D) restored federal protection for Black voters
